abstract: Neural function and survival require a continuous and stable energy supply, relying heavily on efficient ATP production through oxidative phosphorylation1. While this enabled the evolution of fundamental activities such as rapid neuronal communication and synaptic plasticity, it renders neurons uniquely vulnerable to metabolic failure. 'Anoxia depolarization', the hallmark of metabolic injury2, occurs when insufficient ATP triggers an excitotoxic cascade that disrupts ion homeostasis and culminates in neuronal death in most vertebrates. Here, we uncover a paradoxical exception to these rules of neuronal metabolism: the chicken brain. With the highest metabolic rate and body temperature among vertebrates (the highest energetic demand)3, birds would be expected to have a greater vulnerability to metabolic stress. However, upon severe hypoxia, chicken neurons hyperpolarize or maintain membrane potential, preserving ionic regulation and revealing intrinsic neuronal resilience to oxygen deprivation. Building on birds' intriguing physiological capacities4, our findings suggest fundamentally distinct solutions to energetic stress, offering new insights into the evolution of neuronal metabolism and potential avenues for neuroprotection.
